sanjna_rules.description: सेट्/अनिट्/वेट् classification, explained in the book's own opening rules (PDF p.121) before any लकार-specific content.
rules: In आर्धधातुक लकारs there is no vikaraṇa distinction -- forms are produced for all roots by directly joining the relevant प्रत्यय. But there is a peculiarity caused by the इट्-आगम: between some roots and प्रत्ययs, the letter इ is inserted. This letter is called इट्.
Roots that take this इट् augment necessarily are called सेट् (स + इट्, 'with इट्'), e.g. भू (सेट्) → भविता.
Roots that do NOT take इट् are called अनिट् (अन् + इट्, 'without इट्'), e.g. लभ् (अनिट्) → लब्धा.
Roots that take इट् optionally are called वेट् (वा + इट्), e.g. स्यन्द् (वेट्) → स्यन्दिता / स्यन्ता.
These terms (सेट्/वेट्/अनिट्) are noted at the end of each root's citation throughout this प्रकरण.
Some roots take substitutes (आदेश) in आर्धधातुक लकारs: (i) अस् (2nd conj., भुवि) takes substitute भू, e.g. लिट् बभूव. (ii) हू takes substitute वच्, e.g. लिट् उवाच.

special_root_rules: In परस्मैपद, ALL roots reject the इ augment in आशीर्लिङ्; no गुण or वृद्धि takes place either, e.g. भू+यात्=भूयात् (not भो+यात्).
The following roots change their final letter to ए in आशीर्लिङ् (परस्मैपद): दा→देयात्, धा→धेयात्, मा→मेयात्, स्था→स्थेयात्, पा(पाने)→पेयात्, हा→हेयात्.

Roots ending in आ (original or as a substitute) preceded by a conjunct consonant optionally change their final आ to ए: ग्लै(ग्ला)→ग्लेयात्/ग्लायात्, म्लै(म्ला)→म्लेयात्/म्लायात्, ध्यै(ध्या)→ध्येयात्/ध्यायात्, प्रा→प्रेयात्/प्रायात्.
Roots ending in ऋ when preceded by conjunct consonants, and the root वृ, optionally admit इ: स्तृ→स्तरिषीष्ट/स्तृषीष्ट, नृ(?)→नरिषीष्ट/नॄषीष्ट, वृ→वरिषीष्ट/वृषीष्ट.
The following roots drop their penultimate nasal in आशीर्लिङ्: अञ्ज्→अज्यात्, ग्रन्थ्→ग्रथ्यात्, वन्ध्(बन्ध्)→बध्यात्, मन्थ्→मथ्यात्, तृंह्→तृहात्.

rules: लिट् is of two kinds: द्वित्वलिट् (Reduplicative Perfect) and अनुप्रयोगलिट् (Periphrastic Perfect).
In द्वित्वलिट्, the root undergoes द्वित्व (reduplication), e.g. पत्+अ=पपात.
In अनुप्रयोगलिट्, the root combines with the लिट्-forms of भू, अस्, कृ (बभूव, आमास, आञ्चकार), e.g. कथ्→कथयामास / कथयाञ्चकार (कथय्+आम्+बभूव type periphrasis).
Some roots take ONLY द्वित्वलिट्, some ONLY अनुप्रयोगलिट्, and some take both.
Roots of more than one syllable (अनेकाच् धातवः, e.g. दरिद्रा, गवेष्, चकास्) generally take ONLY अनुप्रयोगलिट्, as do the roots द्युत्, अय्, अकास्.
The roots उष्, विद्, जागृ, भी, ह्री, भृ, हु, दरिद्रा take BOTH kinds of लिट्.
All other roots take ONLY द्वित्वलिट्.

dvitva_lit.usage_note: The 2nd and 1st person forms of लिट् are rarely used in modern/classical Sanskrit. In the 1st person, the perfect denotes some distraction or unconscious state of mind and is used mainly in that special sense, e.g. बहु जगद पुरस्तात्तस्य मत्ता किलाहम् ('being much excited, I certainly talked much before him'), or to conceal the truth from somebody, e.g. नाहं कलिङ्गान् जगाम ('I did not go to the Kalingas' -- implying the speaker actually knows they did, in a euphemistic/concealing sense).
